testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Otoe Sub-agency, Red Rock Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of fee patent Indians at Otoe Sub-agency
testimony.key_claims: Fee patent Indians are not as well off as when under Government control. Those who sold land spent money on expensive automobiles, Indian toggery, and gambling. Old dependent Indians receiving $100/month are scarcely able to exist because funds are divided among so many. Indians prefer $10,000 in hand to promise of $100 next week. Recommends turning loose able-bodied and well-educated Indians while establishing a community system for uneducated and old dependent ones. Would reserve 20 acres for a home from individual funds before turning over property.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of fee patent Indians at Pawnee Agency
testimony.key_claims: Going too fast in releasing Indians from Government supervision. Named individuals doing well: Louis Matlock, Eva N. Cummings. Named individuals in this class and some in bad shape: George Haymond, Jobie Taylor, Wilber Eaves, Gorden Shaw, Henry Chapman, Willie Lewis, Robert Peters, James Little Sun, Joe Taylor, Elmer Echo Hawk. Recommends giving fee patent but reserving 40 acres; if individual found capable after investigation, might be given full fee patent. Majority very anxious to get liberty then sorry of outcome.

testimony.witness_title: Agent Farmer, Pawnee Agency, Pawnee Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of fee patent Indians at Pawnee Agency
testimony.key_claims: Indians that received fee patents sold their land and spent all money and are in debt. Not one out of ten who have not sold their land. Some satisfied with how they spent money; others see they made a mistake. Recommends issuing fee patent for part of allotment and holding at least 40 acres in trust. Very few who received fee patent to allotments still own them today. Department gave out about 81 patents; not more than 10 still have their land.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of Sac and Fox and Iowa patented Indians under Shawnee Agency
testimony.key_claims: Acknowledges receipt of circular letter March 24 1921. Those who gained from fee patents: Emmit Pearson (Ralston OK), George Gover (Pawnee OK), Frank Rouwalk (Pawnee OK). Those who have not gained: Clarence Field, Wallace Murie, Caroline Murie, Maggie Knife Chief, Thomas Hand, John Howell, Maude Hand (all Pawnee OK). Most have disposed of allotments and must labor. Not easy for Indian to secure position because whites claim Indians won't work. Most have heired lands to fall back on. Some children do not have necessaries of life. Recommends not turning loose all at once; allow young people who finish education to have property turned over.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Cantonment Agency, Eagle City Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of Cheyenne and Arapahoe fee patent Indians
testimony.key_claims: Worked in Government service three years with Cheyenne and Arapahoe Indians. Only a few have kept land after receiving patent; nearly all sell as soon as they can and run through money but are satisfied and go to work and make better citizens. Named Indians with land under Government control making success of farming: David Bighead, Harry Bates, Walter Fire, Dan Tucker. Named 13 Indians living about Avery and Cushing Oklahoma who sold land after receiving patents. Recommends allowing disposal of heired lands while holding own allotments; portion of miners' interests in heired lands to be deposited and draw interest until of age.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Spokane Indian Agency, Wellpinit Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Fee patents to Spokane Indians; releasing Indians from Government supervision
testimony.key_claims: 112 Indians received fee patents for original allotments. Patents issued 1910-1921. 54 fee patent Indians retained original allotments; 48 sold. Most of 54 retaining are farming own lands; few women leasing. Condition of those who sold is as good as when they held lands. Cannot recall that any are dissatisfied. Does not believe Indians of Spokane Reservation released too soon. Spokane allotments mostly 80 acres or less, mostly timber not valuable, not worth more than $400-$800 after timber cut. Does not think good policy to make all Indians full citizens at once based on blood quantum; each case should be decided on its merits considering education, business experience, degree of blood, robustness, and age. Recommends holding 20 to 40 acres in trust for homesite.

testimony.witness_title: Farmer, Spokane Indian Agency, Wellpinit Washington
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of fee patent Indians on Spokane Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Larger percent of fee patent Indians on Spokane Reservation doing as well as before Government control. Most satisfied with receiving patents. Larger percent of those who sold used money to good advantage. Would examine each case individually. Names of those who sold and are getting along: Del Brown (Miles WA - renting place, interest in sawmill), Caulette Ford (Chewelah WA - built house), Albert Sochemtioken/Garry (Wellpinit WA - sold for $3000 and auto, spent money but has $1000 due and still has car, good worker), Daniel Sherwood (Wellpinit WA - bought better place), Duncan Desautel (Lincoln WA - sold and lived up money but making good living). Those still holding land: John Inkster Jr. (Ford WA - renting allotments of two old Indians, good farming).

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, United States Indian Service, Poteau Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Full removal of restrictions from Choctaw Indians and Five Tribes
testimony.key_claims: Government's work in Five Tribes has been to divide tribes' common estate and vest in each Indian his proportionate share. Blood quantum alone should not determine management of individual case. Considers character, education especially business experience, degree of blood, robustness, age, and circumstances. Many should have restrictions retained indefinitely especially those in out-of-the-way places retaining old tribal customs. Considerable number are reasonably competent. Between 50 and 75 percent have made a success. Most failures come from easy money - Indian regards freedom as windfall of ready cash rather than life responsibility. Drink usually plays big part in failures. Dependents of allottee should weigh heavily in decision. Believes best that 20 to 40 acres be held in trust for homesite. Recommends removing restrictions from inherited land as soon as heirs determined.

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Kiowa Indian Agency, Anadarko Oklahoma
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Patents-in-fee at Kiowa Indian Agency; administrative policy on issuance
testimony.key_claims: Most important administrative function of Indian superintendent is deciding whether to recommend favorably on application for patent-in-fee. Granting patent prematurely subjects Indian to temptation to dissipate estate and acquire extravagant habits. Withholding patent from competent Indian robs him of experience. Always felt it better to err by delaying patent than granting too soon. Does not think good policy to issue patents based on blood quantum or educational qualifications alone. Has full-blood Indians who cannot speak English who are more competent than some with small Indian blood. Of last 60 patents issued under Declaration of Policy: 20 promptly mortgaged (only 1 released), 16 sold outright, 24 so far clear. In 6+ years cannot recall but one case where Indian made a success handling land, and that success could have been achieved under trust. Proposes Government make every Indian select 40 acres as inalienable homestead by Act of Congress, taxable after trust period but taxes not collectable from that property. Allows inherited land restrictions to be removed as heirs determined. Does not believe there are half a dozen of several hundred patents granted who are as competent as average white man.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Condition of fee patent Indians and releasing Indians from Government supervision, from perspective of a Sioux Indian
testimony.key_claims: Testimony content not fully legible in document but referenced as one of the letters included in Bulletin No. 145 from a Sioux Indian relative to releasing Indians from Government supervision.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners inquiry on condition of fee patent Indians
testimony.subject: Views on issuance of patents as embodied in recent letter to Indian Service farmers
testimony.key_claims: All that has been told about Indians selling their lands and wasting proceeds is only too true and only a portion of it has been heard. Private property as represented by Indian allotments has been one of most stable institutions of civilization. Submitting views on issuance of patents.

taxes.context: C.V. Stinchecum proposed that 40-acre homestead held inalienable be made taxable at end of trust period but taxes could not be collected from that property; would be chargeable to any other property Indian might own
Irvine noted loss of taxation to State by reason of land held under restrictions; suggested offset through taxability provisions

taxes.land_description: fee patented allotments sold after receiving patent
taxes.context: Charles B. Thompson noted that releasing Indians from Government control would be a relief to the tax payer; implies fee patent Indians and their destitution create public burden

mortgages.borrower: 20 of last 60 Kiowa Agency patent recipients
mortgages.context: Of last 60 patents issued under Declaration of Policy, 20 were promptly mortgaged; only 1 of those 20 has been released from mortgage; 16 tracts sold outright; 24 so far clear. Reported by C.V. Stinchecum, Superintendent Kiowa Indian Agency.

mortgages.borrower: Indians who received fee patents generally
mortgages.context: Multiple field officers reported that Indians mortgaged their land immediately upon receiving patent-in-fee, including Stinchecum noting mortgaging as one of the primary mechanisms of land loss after fee patent issuance.

mortgages.borrower: fee patent Indians at Pawnee Agency area
mortgages.context: H.F. Furry reported that Indians who received fee patents sold their land, spent all money, and are in debt; consistent with mortgaging pattern.

mortgages.borrower: fee patent Indians on Spokane Reservation who mortgaged
